newsitem.title: USA: U.S. surgeon DeBakey leaves for Russia.
newsitem.headline: U.S. surgeon DeBakey leaves for Russia.

text.p: Famed American heart surgeon Michael DeBakey left for Moscow on Saturday in preparation for surgery next week on ailing Russian President Boris Yeltsin.
DeBakey, 88, was to arrive in the Russian capital on Sunday, then consult with Yeltsin's own medical team the following day.

He said the heart bypass surgery, a procedure that he pioneered in 1964, was expected to take place "early next week," but could not be more specific because of restrictions imposed by Russian officials.
Yeltsin, recovering from earlier heart attacks, was at a sanatorium outside Moscow to gather strength for the surgery. He has made few public appearances since his re-election on July 3.

DeBakey told the Los Angeles Times that he had been informed that Yeltsin's daughter, Tatiana Dyachenko, was behind the secrecy surrounding the date of the operation. Dyachenko has been serving as a liaison between her father and the Kremlin.
"It's stupid to think you can keep this secret. It's so much better to be open, honest and truthful," he said.

Officials at Methodist Hospital here, where DeBakey performs his operations, said he was to be accompanied to Moscow by three Houston-based physicians -- pathologist David Yawn, hematologist Clarence Alfrey and cardiovascular surgeon George Noon.
DeBakey was alone when he entered the Houston airport on Saturday and said he did not know if the others were on the same flight.
"They're supposed to go, but I don't know whether they're on this flight or not. They made their own arrangements. They were requested to come for a consultation for special purposes," DeBakey said.
He said he and the other Houston-based doctors were to serve only as consultants for the operation, which will be a multiple bypass surgery to improve bloodflow to Yeltsin's heart.
"We're not going to be a part of the operation. The Russian team is doing the operation, always has been. We're consultants," he said.

Russian cardiologist Renat Akchurin, who trained under DeBakey at Houston's Baylor College of Medicine, will perform the operation, DeBakey said. Akchurin was in Houston recently to familiarize himself with equipment and procedures that DeBakey uses in his practice.

DeBakey, who examined Yeltsin in September, said then that he expected the Russian leader to make a full recovery, but recommended that he rest and be treated for thyroid problems and anaemia before the surgery.
He told reporters on Saturday that Yeltsin would return to "full duty" no more than two months after the operation.
